questions.q:
Riya and Kabir measure the length of their classroom's back wall by walking heel to toe along it. Riya counts 40 foot-lengths and Kabir counts 32. A ruler shows that Riya's foot is 20 cm long. The class wants a floor mat as long as the wall, and the shop closes this evening; the next delivery is in two weeks, after the class event.
(a) What is the length of the wall in metres?
(b) How long is Kabir's foot?
(c) The shopkeeper's own foot is 32 cm. If the class phones in '40 feet' and he measures with his own foot, how long a mat will he cut, and by how much too long?
(d) Should the class phone the order in today in metres, or wait to measure with a tape? Justify using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) 40 x 20 cm = 800 cm = 8 m. (b) 800 cm / 32 = 25 cm. (c) 40 x 32 cm = 1280 cm = 12.8 m, which is 4.8 m too long. (d) Phone today in metres (8 m). '40 feet' means a different length to each person, as (c) shows with a 4.8 m error, while 8 m worked out from a ruler-measured foot is a standard length that is off by only a little; waiting for a tape would miss the event.
s: Part (a): 8 m
Part (b): 25 cm
Part (c): 12.8 m, 4.8 m too long
Part (d): order 8 m today, because a standard unit means the same to the shopkeeper

questions.q: A blackboard is 2.2 m long. Five friends measure it with their handspans and get 9, 9.5, 10, 10.5 and 11 handspans. Whose handspan is 20 cm long?
questions.a: The friend who counted 11 handspans

questions.q: True or False? 'Padma counted exactly 13 handspans for the table, while the others got slightly more than 13, slightly less than 13, between 13 and 14, and 14. So Padma's measurement is the correct one and the rest are wrong.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Every count is a correct measurement in that person's own handspan; Padma's is a whole number only because the table happens to fit her handspan about 13 times. No count is 'the' correct one, because each was made with a different-sized unit.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: each count is right for that person's own handspan; a whole number is not more correct, the units simply differ

questions.q:
Measuring the same classroom table, Hardeep counted 14 handspans and Padma counted 13. Hardeep's handspan is 15 cm.
Assertion (A): The table is about 2.1 m long.
Reason (R): The longer the unit, the fewer times it fits into the same length.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Padma's handspan is 15 cm long and she measured the classroom table as 13 handspans.
(a) Find the length of the table in centimetres.
(b) Hardeep counted 14 handspans for the same table. Is his handspan longer or shorter than Padma's, and about how long is it (to the nearest centimetre)?
questions.a: (a) 13 x 15 cm = 195 cm. (b) Shorter, because more of his handspans fit; 195 cm / 14 is about 13.9 cm, so about 14 cm.
s: Part (a): 195 cm from 13 x 15 cm
Part (b): shorter, about 14 cm (195 / 14)

questions.q: At a museum, Isha sees a strip of shell from a Harappan site with evenly spaced ruled marks on it. Her brother claims, 'This proves the Harappans used the metre.' Which conclusion does the chapter actually support?
questions.a: It may have been a scale, so length was measured long ago
o: It may have been a scale, so length was measured long ago
It proves the Harappans used the metre, as its marks are evenly spaced
It proves the angula is exactly as long as one of its marked spaces
It cannot be a scale, as standard units were adopted only recently

questions.q: After the table activity, Tasneem says, 'Our readings were slightly more than 13, 13, slightly less than 13, between 13 and 14, and 14 handspans. So the length of the table must have changed while we measured.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. The table did not change. The counts differ because the five handspans are of different sizes, which the friends confirmed by placing their handspans side by side. This is why a unit that does not differ from person to person is needed.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Cause: the handspans (the units) differ in size, not the table
Conclusion: need for a unit that is the same for everyone

questions.q: Meena's stride is 60 cm long and her brother's is 45 cm. Her brother paces out a vegetable bed and counts 20 strides. If Meena paces out the same bed, she will count ___ strides.

Four students measure a 180 cm long bench with their handspans. Their handspans are: Arjun 12 cm, Bela 15 cm, Chirag 16 cm and Divya 18 cm.
(a) Work out each student's count of handspans for the bench.
(b) Who gets the largest count and who the smallest? Explain the pattern.
(c) Chirag reports '11 handspans'. What has he left out, and why does it matter?
(d) Using these results, justify why people agreed on a common standard unit.
questions.a: (a) Arjun 180/12 = 15, Bela 180/15 = 12, Chirag 180/16 = 11.25, Divya 180/18 = 10 handspans. (b) Arjun (shortest handspan) gets the largest count, Divya (longest) the smallest: the shorter the unit, the more times it fits. (c) He has dropped the leftover quarter of a handspan (11.25), so his record makes the bench about 4 cm shorter than it is (0.25 x 16 cm); the leftover part must be shown, for example 'slightly more than 11'. (d) The same bench gives four different numbers, so a count in handspans cannot be shared; a unit that is the same for everyone gives one number for one length.
s: Part (a): all four counts correct (15, 12, 11.25, 10)
Part (b): shortest unit gives largest count, with the reason
Part (c): the leftover quarter handspan (about 4 cm) is lost
Part (d): one length, four numbers, so a common standard unit is needed

questions.q:
Statement 1: In the reading '13 handspans', 13 is the unit and 'handspan' is the number.
Statement 2: The angula, a finger width, is still used by traditional craftspeople such as carpenters and tailors.
Statement 3: Body-based units are unreliable mainly because they are too small to measure a classroom table.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only

questions.q:
A customer orders a shelf 'six handspans long'. Her handspan is 18 cm; the carpenter's is 20 cm.
(a) What length, in centimetres, does the customer actually want?
(b) If the carpenter uses his own handspan, how long will the shelf be, how much too long is that, and what should the order have said instead?
questions.a: (a) 6 x 18 cm = 108 cm. (b) 6 x 20 cm = 120 cm, which is 120 - 108 = 12 cm too long, because a handspan differs from person to person; the order should have given the length in a standard unit, 108 cm.
s: Part (a): 108 cm
Part (b): 120 cm, 12 cm too long; the order should say 108 cm

questions.q: For the same school corridor, Ravi writes 'Length = 42' and Sana writes 'Length = 28'. The teacher has checked that both counted carefully. What best explains the two records?
questions.a: Each counted a different unit and left it out
o: Each counted a different unit and left it out
One of them miscounted, as the corridor stayed the same
Sana used a shorter unit, since her number is smaller
Ravi was more careful, which is why his number is larger

questions.q: A shop record reads: 'Rope sold: 12 arm-lengths at Rs 10 per arm-length.' Write a short situation (two or three lines) in which the buyer and the seller disagree about this sale, then explain the cause of the disagreement and how it could be avoided.
questions.a: E.g. The seller measures 12 of his own long arm-lengths; at home the buyer's son measures the rope as 14 of his shorter arm-lengths and says the price is unfair. Cause: an arm-length differs from person to person, so the count depends on who measures. Remedy: measure the rope in metres with a measuring tape and price it per metre.
s: A realistic disagreement over the count
Cause: the arm-length differs from person to person
Remedy: a standard unit such as the metre

questions.q:
Kavi measures a classroom wall as 20 of his handspans; his handspan is 15 cm. Mitu measures the same wall as 24 of her handspans.
(a) Find the length of the wall in metres from Kavi's data.
(b) Mitu now measures the wall with a metre scale, placed correctly. What will she get, and why will it agree with Kavi's result when her handspan count did not?
questions.a: (a) 20 x 15 cm = 300 cm = 3 m. (b) About 3 m. The metre is the same for everyone, so the same wall gives the same number; a handspan differs from person to person, which is why 20 and 24 differed.
s: Part (a): 300 cm = 3 m
Part (b): about 3 m, because a standard unit does not differ from person to person

questions.q: A school wants every class to chalk a relay line exactly the same distance from the start. Which plan would NOT give identical lines in every class?
questions.a: Each teacher walks ten of her own strides
o: Each teacher walks ten of her own strides
Each class uses the same measuring tape from the sports room
Each class lays one metre scale along the ground ten times
Each class measures with its own metre scale of the same make

questions.q:
Deepa's school skirt is 85 cm long, and her mother tells the tailor to add 'char angula'. The tailor's finger width is 2.0 cm; her mother's is 1.6 cm. The tailor will stitch from whatever length is written on the order slip.
(a) How much length does the tailor add if he uses his own fingers?
(b) What would the new length be if her mother's fingers were used?
(c) By how much do the two versions of 'char angula' differ?
(d) Should the slip say 'add char angula' or give the new length in centimetres? Justify, keeping in mind that tailors still use the angula.
questions.a: (a) 4 x 2.0 cm = 8 cm. (b) 85 cm + 4 x 1.6 cm = 85 + 6.4 = 91.4 cm. (c) 8 cm - 6.4 cm = 1.6 cm. (d) Give the new length in centimetres. The angula is a familiar working unit for tailors and is quick to show with the fingers, but it differs from person to person; since the two versions differ by 1.6 cm, writing the new length (for example 93 cm) in centimetres removes the doubt about whose fingers are meant.
s: Part (a): 8 cm
Part (b): 91.4 cm
Part (c): 1.6 cm
Part (d): centimetres, because the two versions of char angula differ by 1.6 cm

questions.q:
Deepa records the table as 'between 13 and 14 handspans'.
(a) Why could she not write a whole number?
(b) Without using a scale, suggest how she could state the length more exactly, and write a sample record.
questions.a: (a) The table is longer than 13 of her handspans but shorter than 14, so a part of a handspan is left over at the end. (b) Measure the leftover part with a smaller body unit, such as finger widths (angula), and write both, e.g. '13 handspans and 3 angula'.
s: Part (a): a leftover part smaller than one handspan
Part (b): measure the leftover with a smaller unit such as the angula, with a sample record

questions.q: Rohit says, 'The angula is a unit found in ancient Indian literature, and it went out of use long ago.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The angula (finger width) is indeed mentioned in ancient Indian literature, and was used in measuring artefacts, architecture and town planning. But it did not go out of use: traditional craftspeople such as carpenters and tailors still use it.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: the angula appears in ancient Indian literature and was used in artefacts, architecture and town planning
Wrong part: carpenters and tailors still use the angula

questions.q: A customer asks a carpenter to make a shelf 'do angula' (two finger widths) deeper than the old one. The customer's finger is 1.5 cm wide and the carpenter's is 2.1 cm. If the carpenter uses his own fingers, how will the new shelf compare with what the customer expects?
questions.a: 1.2 cm deeper
o: The same depth, as both mean do angula

questions.q:
A farmer paces out a strip 20 strides long with his 75 cm stride. His son, whose stride is 50 cm, is sent to mark an identical strip on the other side of the field and is told only '20 strides'.
(a) How long is the farmer's strip in metres?
(b) How long will the son's strip be, and by how many metres will it fall short?
(c) How many of his own strides should the son have taken to match?
(d) Compare the stride method with using a measuring tape for this job and justify which one the farmer should use when two people share the work.
questions.a: (a) 20 x 75 cm = 1500 cm = 15 m. (b) 20 x 50 cm = 1000 cm = 10 m, so 5 m short. (c) 1500 cm / 50 cm = 30 strides. (d) Strides are quick and need no tool, and work when one person does all the marking; but a stride differs from person to person, so when two people share the work a measuring tape (a standard unit) gives the same length for both and should be used.
s: Part (a): 15 m
Part (b): 10 m, 5 m short
Part (c): 30 strides
Part (d): stride method quick but person-dependent; tape gives the same result for both, so the tape is the right choice

questions.q: A railway engineer records that the track between two cities is 412 km long, and a printer records that one sheet of paper is 0.1 mm thick. A clerk must copy both lengths into a register. Which entry is correct and the most convenient to read?
questions.a: 412 km and 0.1 mm

questions.q: Lata's height is 1.68 m. Her younger brother is 23 cm shorter than her. Written in millimetres, his height is ___ mm.
Rewrite this sentence so that every unit follows the chapter's rules, and name two rules you used: 'The ribbon is 45 Cms. long and the table is 2M long.'
questions.a: 'The ribbon is 45 cm long and the table is 2 m long.' Rules: unit symbols are written in lowercase; no 's' is added for the plural and no full stop after the symbol (except at the end of a sentence); leave a space between the number and the unit (any two).
s: Correctly rewritten sentence
Two rules named correctly

questions.q:
Statement 1: 1 mm is one-tenth of a centimetre, so 6 mm = 0.6 cm.
Statement 2: An ordinary 15-cm scale can directly measure a length of 0.5 mm.
Statement 3: Countries adopted a common set of standard units because travel between places using different systems caused confusion.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
A school library shelf is 45.5 cm long. The librarian places 12 books that are each 18 mm thick and 8 books that are each 25 mm thick on it. She would like to add more: dictionaries 25 mm thick or storybooks 18 mm thick.
(a) What length of shelf do the 20 books take up, in millimetres?
(b) How much space is left, in centimetres?
(c) Which of these fit in the space left: two storybooks; one dictionary; one dictionary and one storybook together?
(d) Students ask for the dictionary every day, while the two new storybooks would be borrowed about once a month. What should she add? Give your reasoning.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 18 + 8 x 25 = 216 + 200 = 416 mm. (b) 455 - 416 = 39 mm = 3.9 cm. (c) Two storybooks need 36 mm, which fits; one dictionary needs 25 mm, which fits; a dictionary and a storybook need 43 mm, which does not fit. (d) Add the dictionary. Either choice fits the 39 mm, but not both together, so she must choose; one book used daily serves students more than two books used once a month.
s: Part (a): 416 mm
Part (b): 3.9 cm
Part (c): two storybooks fit (36 mm), one dictionary fits (25 mm), both together do not (43 mm)
Part (d): the dictionary, because only one choice fits and it is used daily

questions.q: A signboard at the start of a trekking path reads '3 km 40 m to the waterfall'. Sunil walks 1850 m along the path and reaches a second signboard. What distance should the second board show?
Four cycle routes are listed as 1.2 km, 1150 m, 125000 cm and 1100000 mm. Arrange them from shortest to longest, showing your conversions.
s: All four converted to one unit
Correct order

questions.q:
(a) The distance from Kiran's house to the stadium is 2.35 km. Express it in metres.
(b) How many full 100 m lengths are there in this distance, and how much is left over?
questions.a: (a) 2.35 x 1000 = 2350 m. (b) 2350 / 100 = 23.5, so 23 full 100 m lengths with 50 m left over.
s: Part (a): 2350 m
Part (b): 23 full lengths and 50 m left over

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The road distance between Delhi and Lucknow is more conveniently stated in kilometres than in metres.
Reason (R): 1 km is equal to 100 m, so the number becomes smaller.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Kiran makes a cheap 'metre scale' by marking 100 equal centimetre divisions on a strip of rubber that is exactly 1 m long when relaxed. She pulls it straight along her desk, and the desk exactly fills the strip from its 0 mark to its 100 mark. When pulled like this the strip is stretched to 104 cm. A steel metre scale shows that the desk is 104 cm long.
(a) What length does Kiran's rubber scale give for the desk?
(b) By how much is that wrong, and is it too long or too short?
(c) How long is each 'centimetre' division on the stretched strip, in millimetres?
(d) Her friend pulls the same strip harder and reads a smaller number for the same desk. Using the idea of a unit, explain why her scale cannot serve as a standard, and say what kind of material a scale needs.
questions.a: (a) 100 cm. (b) 104 - 100 = 4 cm too short. (c) 104 cm / 100 = 1.04 cm = 10.4 mm. (d) Each division changes length with how hard the strip is pulled, so the unit itself is not fixed and different people get different numbers for the same desk; a standard unit must not differ from one measurement to the next, so the scale must be made of a material that does not stretch, such as the steel of the steel metre scale in the question.
s: Part (a): 100 cm
Part (b): 4 cm too short
Part (c): 10.4 mm per division
Part (d): a stretching unit is not fixed, so readings differ; a scale needs a material that does not stretch

questions.q:
Match each length in Column I with the same length written in another unit in Column II.
Column I: 1. 0.23 km  2. 15 mm  3. 1.8 m  4. 4.5 cm
Column II: a. 45 mm  b. 230 m  c. 1.5 cm  d. 180 cm

(a) The highway between two towns is 86 km long. Write this in metres, and say which of the two units is more convenient.
(b) A coin is 2 mm thick. Write this in metres, and say which of the two units is more convenient.
questions.a: (a) 86 x 1000 = 86000 m; the kilometre is more convenient because the number of metres is very large. (b) 2 / 1000 = 0.002 m; the millimetre is more convenient because in metres it is a tiny decimal.
s: Part (a): 86000 m, kilometre preferred
Part (b): 0.002 m, millimetre preferred

questions.q:
Ritika wants the thickness of one sheet of her notebook. The smallest length her 15-cm scale can measure is 1 mm.
(a) A notebook of many sheets is only a few millimetres thick. Show that she cannot read the thickness of one sheet directly.
(b) She presses 200 sheets together and the stack measures 1.6 cm. Find the thickness of one sheet in millimetres.
(c) Explain why measuring the stack works when measuring one sheet does not.
questions.a: (a) If many sheets together are only a few millimetres thick, one sheet is much thinner than 1 mm, so it does not cover even one small division of the scale. (b) 1.6 cm = 16 mm, and 16 mm / 200 = 0.08 mm. (c) The stack is many millimetres thick, so it can be read on the scale; dividing by the number of sheets shares that length equally among them.
s: Part (a): a sheet is thinner than the smallest division, 1 mm
Part (c): the stack is long enough to read, then divide by the number of sheets

questions.q: Ankit measures his eraser with a 15-cm scale whose centimetres are each divided into 10 small parts. He reports '4.25 cm'. What is wrong with his report?
questions.a: The scale cannot show 0.05 cm; it reads to 1 mm, so 4.2 or 4.3 cm
o: The scale cannot show 0.05 cm; it reads to 1 mm, so 4.2 or 4.3 cm
Nothing; each small mark on a 15-cm scale is 0.25 cm from the next
He should write 4.25 mm, since the small parts on the scale are mm
The scale cannot show tenths of a cm, so he should write 4 cm only

questions.q: True or False? 'Raju's old cloth tape is marked in inches on one side and in centimetres on the other. When he measures a ribbon, the reading on either side is a measurement in SI units.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Both sides measure the same ribbon correctly, but only the centimetre reading is in SI units, because the SI unit of length is the metre (and the centimetre is part of it). The inch is an older unit that some people still use; it is not an SI unit.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: only the centimetre side is SI; the inch is an older, non-SI unit

questions.q:
At a cloth shop the shopkeeper measures with a metal measuring rod marked in metres. Deepa's family buys 2 m for her uniform, 1.75 m for her brother and 125 cm for a cushion cover, all cut from one roll holding 6.4 m. The cloth costs Rs 180 per metre.
(a) What is the total length bought, in metres?
(b) What is the bill?
(c) How much cloth is left on the roll, in centimetres?
(d) Mother will need 130 cm more for a table runner next month. The shopkeeper offers the leftover piece now for Rs 250. She will be passing the shop next month anyway and could buy exactly 130 cm at the usual rate then, but the shopkeeper cannot promise that this same cloth will still be in stock. Which would you advise? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) 2 + 1.75 + 1.25 = 5 m. (b) 5 x Rs 180 = Rs 900. (c) 6.4 - 5 = 1.4 m = 140 cm. (d) Buy the leftover now. Waiting costs 1.3 x Rs 180 = Rs 234, only Rs 16 less than the Rs 250 leftover, and the leftover's 140 cm covers the 130 cm needed with 10 cm to spare; paying Rs 16 more is a small price for being sure of matching cloth, which may not be in stock next month. (Waiting is acceptable only if the answer weighs the Rs 16 saving against that risk.)
s: Part (a): 5 m after converting 125 cm
Part (b): Rs 900
Part (c): 140 cm
Part (d): Rs 234 against Rs 250; buy now, as Rs 16 is small against the stock risk

questions.q:
For a craft project Mohan has three pieces of rope: 1.2 m, 85 cm and 450 mm.
(a) Find their total length in centimetres.
(b) He needs 3 m of rope in all. How much more does he need, in metres?
questions.a: (a) 120 cm + 85 cm + 45 cm = 250 cm. (b) 250 cm = 2.5 m, so he needs 3 - 2.5 = 0.5 m more.
s: Part (a): 250 cm after converting each piece
Part (b): 0.5 m more

questions.q: Kavya says, '0.5 km is longer than 450 m, even though 0.5 is a smaller number than 450.' Check her claim with a conversion.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. 0.5 km = 0.5 x 1000 m = 500 m, which is 50 m more than 450 m. A number on its own cannot be compared; lengths must first be in the same unit.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
500 m exceeds 450 m by 50 m; compare only in the same unit

questions.q: Four students write the length of a ribbon that is 2.05 m long. Whose entry is equal to 2.05 m and also follows the rules for writing units?
questions.a: Neha: 205 cm

questions.q:
Jaya walks from home to school, 1.25 km each way, on 6 days a week. On 2 of those days she also walks from school to the library and back to school, 750 m each way.
(a) How far does she walk to and from school in one day?
(b) What is her total walking distance for the week, in kilometres?
(c) Express the weekly total in metres.
(d) Her friend Rekha walks 17500 m in a week. Who walks farther, and by how much? Give the answer in kilometres.
questions.a: (a) 1.25 x 2 = 2.5 km. (b) School: 2.5 x 6 = 15 km; library: 0.75 x 2 x 2 = 3 km; total 18 km. (c) 18 x 1000 = 18000 m. (d) Rekha's 17500 m = 17.5 km, so Jaya walks farther, by 18 - 17.5 = 0.5 km.
s: Part (a): 2.5 km
Part (b): 18 km including the library walks
Part (c): 18000 m
Part (d): 17500 m = 17.5 km, so Jaya, by 0.5 km

questions.q:
Assertion (A): For a pencil about 9.6 cm long, a 15-cm scale is a more convenient choice than a metre scale, although both can measure it.
Reason (R): 1 mm is the smallest length that can be measured with a 15-cm scale.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
(a) A carpenter measures the height of a door with a measuring tape as 2.05 m. His helper lays a metre scale end to end up the door: two full lengths, and then the top of the door is at the 5 cm mark on the third placement. He writes 205 cm. Do they agree? Show it.
(b) A third person lays a 15-cm scale end to end up the door about 14 times and gets 208 cm. Suggest why this result is the odd one out.
questions.a: (a) Yes: helper's reading = 100 + 100 + 5 = 205 cm, and 2.05 m = 2.05 x 100 = 205 cm, so they agree. (b) A 15-cm scale is not an appropriate scale for a door; laying it about 14 times gives about 14 chances to leave a gap or overlap or to slip, so small errors add up.
s: Part (a): 100 + 100 + 5 = 205 cm and 2.05 m = 205 cm, so they agree
Part (b): too short a scale; many placements let errors add up

questions.q: Three students read the tip of the same pencil on a scale. Anu, looking from the left at a slant, reads 8.8 cm; Bilal, with his eye directly above the tip, reads 8.4 cm; Chitra, looking from the right at a slant, reads 8.3 cm. Chitra suggests recording the average of all three. What would that record, and is it acceptable?
questions.a: 8.5 cm; not acceptable, two readings break the eye-position rule
o: 8.5 cm; not acceptable, two readings break the eye-position rule
8.4 cm; acceptable, since averaging always cancels the slanting errors
8.5 cm; acceptable, since it uses every student's reading of the tip
8.3 cm; not acceptable, since Chitra's own reading is the smallest one

questions.q: Arif says, 'If my scale's zero is broken and I start the object at the 1.0 cm mark, I should add 1 cm to the reading at the other end.' Check his claim with an example.
questions.a: No. Starting at 1.0 cm means the scale has already counted 1 cm before the object begins, so 1.0 cm must be subtracted, not added. Example: object from 1.0 cm to 10.4 cm is 10.4 - 1.0 = 9.4 cm; adding would give 11.4 cm, which is 2 cm too long.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Reason: the starting reading must be subtracted
A worked example showing the difference

questions.q:
In a leaf-measuring activity, three students read the length of the same leaf with a 15-cm scale. Kiran, with her eye directly above the tip, reads 8.4 cm; Lalit, looking from one side, reads 8.7 cm; Manju, looking from the other side, reads 8.1 cm. The group of five must now record 30 leaves in one 20-minute lesson, and a careful reading takes about 1 minute per leaf.
(a) Which reading of the first leaf should be accepted? Why?
(b) By how much does each side reading differ from the accepted one?
(c) How long would one student take to read all 30 leaves, and how long would it take if the five share them equally?
(d) Should Kiran read all 30 leaves herself, or should the leaves be shared? Justify using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Kiran's 8.4 cm, because her eye was directly above the mark. (b) Lalit's is 0.3 cm too long and Manju's 0.3 cm too short. (c) One student: 30 x 1 = 30 minutes; shared: 30 / 5 = 6 leaves each, about 6 minutes. (d) Share the leaves. Kiran alone needs 30 minutes, more than the 20-minute lesson, while sharing takes about 6 minutes; the errors in (b) came from eye position, so every student must keep the eye directly above the mark, and there is time left for Kiran to recheck some leaves.
s: Part (a): Kiran, eye directly above
Part (b): 0.3 cm each way
Part (c): 30 minutes alone, 6 minutes shared
Part (d): share, since one reader cannot finish in 20 minutes, with the eye-position rule

questions.q: True or False? 'Even when every student uses the same metre scale, two students measuring the same table can get different readings if one of them reads the mark from a slant.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The eye must be directly above the mark being read; looking from a slant gives a wrong reading, so a standard scale alone does not guarantee the same result.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a reading taken from a slant is wrong; the eye must be directly above the mark

questions.q: Gopal must measure two things in the school garden: the girth (distance round) of a neem tree, about 1.5 m, and the length of a straight boundary wall, about 9 m. He may borrow only ONE of these: a 15 m flexible measuring tape, a metre scale, or a 30-cm scale. Which should he borrow?
questions.a: The flexible tape: it bends round the trunk and spans the wall
o: The flexible tape: it bends round the trunk and spans the wall
The metre scale: it is rigid, so both of its readings will stay accurate
The 30-cm scale: its fine millimetre marks make both readings exact
Any one of the three, since each is marked in standard units of length

questions.q:
Ayesha is visually challenged and measures lengths with a scale that has raised markings.
(a) Why can she not use an ordinary printed scale, and how do the raised markings help?
(b) Of the two precautions in the chapter (placing the scale and positioning the eye), which one does she certainly still need while using her raised-marking scale? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) She cannot see printed marks; raised markings can be felt by touching them, so she reads the scale by touch. (b) She still needs to place the scale in contact with the object along its length, because that decides which mark lines up with the end of the object, whether the mark is read by eye or by touch.
s: Part (a): marks are felt by touch
Part (b): placing the scale in contact along the length is still needed, with reason

questions.q:
A Class 6 worksheet has four measuring records:
P: 'Pencil: scale placed touching it along its length, one end at 0, eye directly above the tip: 11.2 cm.'
Q: 'Matchbox: scale held about 2 cm above it, eye directly above each end: 5.3 cm.'
R: 'My brother's chest: metre scale held against it: 70 cm.'
S: 'Notebook length: scale laid from one corner to the opposite corner: 29.4 cm.'
(a) Which record was taken correctly?
(b) What precaution was broken in Q, and what should be done?
(c) Why can R not be trusted, and what should have been used?
(d) What is wrong with S, and how should the notebook be measured?
(e) Explain why P alone can be trusted even though all four students used standard units.
questions.a: (a) P. (b) The scale was not placed in contact with the matchbox; it must touch the object along its length. (c) A chest is curved and a rigid metre scale cannot follow it; a flexible measuring tape such as a tailor's tape should be used. (d) The scale was laid across the corners, not along the length; it should be placed along the long edge, touching it. (e) A standard unit only makes results agree when the right instrument is placed and read correctly; Q, R and S each broke one of these, so only P gives the true length.
s: Part (a): P
Part (b): scale not in contact; place it touching along the length
Part (c): curved chest needs a flexible tape
Part (d): scale not along the length; place it along the edge
Part (e): standard units need the right instrument used correctly

questions.q: Meena measures a windowsill with her 15-cm scale, moving it along. By mistake she starts the second placement 0.5 cm before the point where the first one ended, so the two placements overlap. She counts two full placements and then reads 11.5 cm on the third, and writes 41.5 cm. What is the true length of the windowsill?
questions.a: 41 cm

questions.q: A pencil is placed with one end at the 0 mark of a 15-cm scale. Its tip lies exactly 3 small divisions short of the 10 cm mark. The pencil is ___ cm long.

To keep a drawn line visible, Sana holds her scale above the paper, slightly tilted, keeps her eye directly above each end of the line and reads 6.4 cm. Imran lays the same scale flat on the paper, touching the line along its length, and reads 6.0 cm. Sana says, 'My eye was in the right place, so my reading is as good as his.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. The length is 6.0 cm; Sana's reading is 6.4 - 6.0 = 0.4 cm too long. Keeping the eye directly above the mark is only one precaution; the chapter also says to place the scale in contact with the object along its length. A raised, tilted scale does not lie along the line, so its marks do not sit against the ends, and more of the scale is used up between the ends than the line's true length.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong; 6.0 cm is the length, 0.4 cm difference
The scale must also be placed in contact along the length
A raised, tilted scale does not lie along the line, so the reading comes out too long

questions.q: Four students measure the same key with an ordinary 15-cm scale marked in centimetres and millimetres. Which record could NOT have been read from this scale?

Rima and Joy each measure the same comb with the same metre scale and get 12.6 cm. Sam gets 12.9 cm with the same scale.
(a) Give one likely mistake in the way Sam measured.
(b) Earlier, the friends' handspan counts of a table differed because their units differed. Explain why that cannot be the reason this time.
questions.a: (a) He may have read the mark from a slant instead of directly above it, or not placed the scale in contact along the comb (either one). (b) All three used the same metre scale, so the unit, the centimetre, was the same for everyone; only a reading or placing mistake can explain the difference.
s: Part (a): a reading or placing mistake (eye not above the mark, or scale not in contact)
Part (b): the centimetre is the same for all, so the unit is not the cause

questions.q:
For a science display, Meera must report three lengths of a clay pot: its height (about 25 cm), the distance round its widest part, and the thickness of its rim (about 6 mm). She has a 15-cm scale, a metre scale and a thread.
(a) Which instrument should she use for the height, and why not the 15-cm scale?
(b) Describe how she will find the distance round the widest part.
(c) Her readings are: height 24.6 cm; the marked thread reaches the 58.3 cm mark on the metre scale, starting from 0; rim 6 mm. Write all three in millimetres.
(d) Which unit is the most convenient for each of the three lengths? Give a reason for the rim.
questions.a: (a) The metre scale: the pot is about 25 cm tall, longer than a 15-cm scale, so the 15-cm scale would have to be moved and read twice. (b) Wrap the thread once round the widest part, mark where it meets its start, straighten it and read it against the metre scale with the eye directly above the mark. (c) Height 246 mm; distance round 583 mm; rim 6 mm. (d) Centimetres for the height and the distance round; millimetres for the rim, because it is less than 1 cm and would be a decimal (0.6 cm) in centimetres.
s: Part (a): metre scale, the pot is taller than 15 cm
Part (b): thread wrapped, marked, straightened and read
Part (c): 246 mm, 583 mm and 6 mm
Part (d): cm for the large lengths, mm for the rim with reason

questions.q: Raju places a 15-cm scale correctly along a pencil, with one end at the 0 mark and his eye directly above the tip, and reads 11.2 cm. Lata measures the same pencil correctly with a metre scale, but because the start of her scale is covered with tape, she puts the back end of the pencil exactly at the 20 cm mark. What reading should she see at the tip?
Neha says, 'As long as I keep my eye directly above the mark, my reading of any length will be correct.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Keeping the eye directly above the mark is needed for a correct reading. But it is not enough: the scale must also be placed in contact with the object along its length, a scale with a broken end needs the starting reading subtracted, and the instrument must suit the length (a rigid scale cannot measure a curved girth).
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: the eye must be directly above the mark
Wrong part: placement, a broken end and the right instrument also matter (any two)

questions.q:
Three friends measure the same eraser. Pooja writes 'Eraser = 4.6'. Nikhil looks at its far end from the side and writes 'Eraser = 4.9 cm'. Tara, with her eye directly above each end, writes 'Eraser = 46 mm'.
(a) Show that Pooja's record agrees with Tara's only if Pooja meant centimetres, and say what her record is missing.
(b) By how much is Nikhil's reading off, and what should he do differently?
questions.a: (a) 46 mm = 46 / 10 = 4.6 cm, so Pooja's 4.6 matches Tara's only as 4.6 cm (4.6 mm would be far smaller than an eraser); her record is missing the unit, and a length needs both a number and a unit. (b) 4.9 - 4.6 = 0.3 cm too long; he should read the mark with his eye directly above the end of the eraser.
s: Part (a): 46 mm = 4.6 cm; the unit is missing
Part (b): 0.3 cm too long; read with the eye directly above the mark

questions.q:
On sports day the long-jump team finds that the first 10 cm of its measuring tape is torn off. The judges hold the 10 cm mark at the take-off board and read the tape at the landing mark: Asha 2.85 m, Bina 3.10 m, Charu 2.97 m. Only jumps of 2.90 m or more qualify for the inter-school meet.
(a) What is Asha's actual jump?
(b) What are Bina's and Charu's actual jumps?
(c) If the judges forget to correct the readings, who would wrongly qualify?
(d) A full tape can be borrowed from the next school, but it will arrive an hour late and delay the final. Should the school use the torn tape with the correction, or wait? Justify using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) 2.85 m - 0.10 m = 2.75 m. (b) Bina 3.00 m, Charu 2.87 m. (c) Charu: her reading 2.97 m looks above 2.90 m, but her actual jump is 2.87 m. (d) Use the torn tape with the correction. Subtracting 0.10 m from every reading gives the true jumps, as (a) and (b) show, so nothing is gained by delaying the final; the only danger is a forgotten subtraction, which (c) shows would wrongly qualify Charu, so a second judge should check each subtraction.
s: Part (a): 2.75 m
Part (b): 3.00 m and 2.87 m
Part (c): Charu would wrongly qualify
Part (d): use the torn tape, subtracting 0.10 m each time with a check, since the correction gives true lengths

questions.q:
Statement 1: A wall 3.2 m long measured with a 15-cm scale, moved along it, needs at least 22 placements of the scale.
Statement 2: A metre scale can directly measure the girth of a tree if it is read with the eye directly above the mark.
Statement 3: If the scale touches a pencil along its length, reading the tip from a slant still gives the correct length.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only

questions.q: Faisal wraps a thread 5 times around a thin water pipe and marks the thread where the fifth turn ends. His scale's zero end is broken, so he straightens the thread along it from the 2.5 cm mark; the pen mark reaches the 50.0 cm mark. What is the distance once around the pipe?
questions.a: 9.5 cm

questions.q: Three students measure the rim of the same round steel plate. Kunal uses a thread and gets 78.5 cm; Leena uses a flexible tape and gets 78.5 cm; Hari lays his 15-cm scale round the rim piece by piece, adds the pieces and gets 74 cm. Hari says, 'My answer is as good as theirs, because I added carefully.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Each straight piece of Hari's scale cuts across a part of the curve instead of following it, so every piece is shorter than the curved part it stands for, and his total comes out short, by 78.5 - 74 = 4.5 cm. Careful adding cannot fix this; the thread and the flexible tape follow the curve, which is why they agree.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Straight pieces cut across the curve, so the total is too short (by 4.5 cm)
The thread and the tape follow the curve, so their matching 78.5 cm is trusted

questions.q: A rangoli border is made of 6 equal curved arcs. A thread is laid along all 6 arcs and straightened along a measuring tape: up to the pen mark it measures 1.62 m. Later it is found that the pen mark was made 6 cm beyond the end of the last arc. Each arc is ___ cm long.

Three lengths are to be measured: (i) the edge of a rectangular table top, (ii) the rim of a round dinner plate, (iii) a garden hose lying on the ground in an S-shape.
(a) Which of them can be measured directly with a metre scale, and which need a thread or a flexible tape? Give the reason.
(b) For the hose, suggest a way that needs neither a thread nor a flexible tape, and say why it works.
questions.a: (a) The table edge is straight, so a metre scale works; the plate rim and the S-shaped hose are curved, so they need a thread or a flexible tape. (b) Pull the hose out straight along the ground and lay the metre scale along it: the hose is flexible like a thread, so straightening it changes its shape but not its length.
s: Part (a): table edge by metre scale; rim and hose need thread or tape, because they are curved
Part (b): straighten the hose itself, since straightening keeps its length

questions.q:
A juice stall wants a paper label to go once around the base of each bottle, with 1 cm extra for overlap. The owner has strips of paper 90 cm long and needs labels for 30 bottles. A thread wrapped once around a bottle's base, marked and straightened, measures 21.5 cm.
(a) Why was a thread used instead of the 15-cm scale?
(b) How long must each label be?
(c) How many labels can be cut from one strip, and how many strips are needed for 30 bottles?
(d) To save paper, a helper wants to drop the 1 cm overlap. Is that worth doing? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) The base is curved; a rigid scale cannot follow it, while a thread can be laid around it, then straightened and measured. (b) 21.5 + 1 = 22.5 cm. (c) 90 / 22.5 = 4 labels per strip; 30 / 4 = 7.5, so 8 strips. (d) Not worth it: without the overlap each label is 21.5 cm and 90 / 21.5 is about 4.2, still only 4 whole labels per strip, so no paper is saved and the labels would not overlap.
s: Part (a): curved base needs a thread
Part (b): 22.5 cm
Part (c): 4 per strip, 8 strips
Part (d): no saving, still 4 labels per strip

questions.q:
Statement 1: A thread that slips and cuts straight across one bend of a curve gives a straightened length longer than the curve.
Statement 2: A flexible measuring tape laid round a bangle can be read directly, with no straightening step.
Statement 3: If a thread wrapped 4 times round a pipe straightens to 30.0 cm, the distance once round the pipe is 7.5 cm.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q: True or False? 'A cotton thread laid along a curved line and then straightened will be shorter than the curve, because straightening removes the bends.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Straightening changes only the shape of the thread, not its length. If the thread followed every bend and was not stretched, its straightened length is equal to the length of the curve.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: straightening changes the shape, not the length, so the lengths are equal

questions.q:
A curved path in a park is to be edged with tiles that are each 30 cm long, laid end to end. The gardener can use either a long thread with a metre scale or the 15 m flexible measuring tape from the sports room.
(a) Which instrument suits a 12-metre-long curved path better? Justify.
(b) The measured length is 12.6 m. How many tiles are needed?
(c) If someone measured the straight gap between the ends of the path instead, would the tiles be too few or too many? Explain.
(d) Justify why straightening a thread is the key step when only a thread and a rigid scale are available.
questions.a: (a) The flexible measuring tape: it follows the curve and is read directly, and it is long enough; a 12 m thread would have to be measured against a metre scale about 12 times, adding chances of error. (b) 1260 cm / 30 cm = 42 tiles. (c) Too few, because the straight gap is shorter than the curved path. (d) A rigid scale can only be read along a straight line, so the thread, after taking the curve's length, must be straightened before it can be laid against the scale.
s: Part (a): tape chosen with a reason
Part (b): 42 tiles
Part (c): too few, straight gap is shorter
Part (d): a rigid scale reads only straight lengths

questions.q: Tanu lays a thread along the curved edge of a paper fan, but by mistake she marks the thread 2.0 cm beyond the point where the edge ends. She straightens the thread and reads 27.0 cm on a metre scale. What is the true length of the curved edge?

Assertion (A): A metre scale is the most suitable instrument for directly measuring the curved arch of a verandah.
Reason (R): A metre scale is rigid and straight.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
Arjun lays a thread along a curved verandah arch and marks it. Instead of straightening it, he holds a 3 m measuring tape straight across from one end of the curved thread to the other and reads 1.6 m. His sister straightens the same marked thread along the tape and reads 2.3 m.
(a) Which value is the length of the arch? Why?
(b) By how much is Arjun's value short, and what would happen if he bought string lights using it?
questions.a: (a) 2.3 m: the straightened thread has the full length of the curve, while Arjun measured only the straight gap between the ends, which cuts across the curve. (b) 2.3 - 1.6 = 0.7 m short; the lights would not reach along the whole arch.
s: Part (a): 2.3 m, because the straight gap cuts across the curve
Part (b): 0.7 m short, so the lights would fall short

questions.q: A student's notebook shows only this line: 'Thread length after straightening = 31.4 cm.' Write a situation that could have produced this record, and list the steps the student followed.
questions.a: E.g. Arnav wanted the length of the curved edge of a clay diya. He laid a thread along the curved edge, marked the thread where the edge ended, straightened it without stretching, and placed it along a metre scale with his eye directly above the mark, reading 31.4 cm.
s: A curved object that suits the record
Steps: lay along curve and mark
Steps: straighten without stretching and read on a rigid scale

questions.q: Ira follows the curve of a jar's base with a rubber band, then stretches the band along a scale to read it. How will her result compare with the real distance around the base?
questions.a: Longer, because the band stretched when she pulled it straight
o: Longer, because the band stretched when she pulled it straight
Shorter, because a rubber band cannot follow a curve
The same, because any flexible material gives the curved length
Shorter, because the scale is rigid and the band is flexible

questions.q:
Match each mistake in measuring a curved line (Column I) with its effect (Column II).
Column I: 1. The thread cuts straight across a bend instead of following it  2. A rubber band is used and stretched on the scale  3. The straightened thread is read from a slant  4. A rigid metre scale is held against the curve
Column II: a. The result comes out longer than the curve  b. The scale cannot follow the curve at all  c. The result comes out shorter than the curve  d. The reading is wrong because the eye is not above the mark

Nisha wraps a thread 3 times around the base of a steel tumbler and marks it where the third turn ends. Straightened, the marked thread is 66.3 cm long.
(a) Find the distance once around the base.
(b) She wants a ribbon that goes round the base twice, with 2 cm extra for a knot. The shop sells ribbon only in whole pieces of 10 cm, 20 cm, 30 cm and so on. What is the shortest piece she can buy, and how much will be left over?
questions.a: (a) 66.3 / 3 = 22.1 cm. (b) 2 x 22.1 + 2 = 46.2 cm is needed, so the shortest piece is 50 cm, leaving 50 - 46.2 = 3.8 cm over.
s: Part (a): 22.1 cm
Part (b): 46.2 cm needed, so a 50 cm piece, 3.8 cm left over

questions.q:
For a celebration, Anish's family will hang string lights along the 3 arches of their verandah and then 1.5 m more down to the socket. Each arch is the same size. The thread was laid along the arches in a hurry, so the true total could be up to 0.5 m more than measured. Lights are sold in 5 m strands at Rs 350 or 3 m strands at Rs 230; strands can be joined end to end.
(a) The thread laid along one arch is longer than their metre scale. Laid along the scale, it covers the full scale once, then a second time, and the pen mark finally reaches the 40 cm mark. How long is each arch?
(b) What total length of lights is needed?
(c) Compare the cost and the spare length of two 5 m strands with three 3 m strands.
(d) Which would you buy? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) 1 m + 1 m + 40 cm = 2.4 m. (b) 3 x 2.4 + 1.5 = 8.7 m. (c) Two 5 m strands: Rs 700 for 10 m, 1.3 m spare; three 3 m strands: Rs 690 for 9 m, 0.3 m spare. (d) Two 5 m strands. The three 3 m strands save only Rs 10, but their 0.3 m spare is less than the 0.5 m the hurried measurement may have missed, so they might not reach; the 5 m strands leave 1.3 m spare and need one join instead of two.
s: Part (a): 2.4 m
Part (b): 8.7 m
Part (c): Rs 700 with 1.3 m spare against Rs 690 with 0.3 m spare
Part (d): two 5 m strands, since 0.3 m spare may not cover a 0.5 m shortfall

questions.q: Zara's rangoli border has one straight edge and one curved edge. She measures the straight edge with a metre scale: 45.0 cm. She lays a thread along the curved edge, marks it and straightens it along the same metre scale: it covers the whole scale once and then reaches the 38.5 cm mark. What is the total length of the border?
Kunal says, 'For every curved length a thread is better than a flexible tape, because a thread is cheaper and can be read at once.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. A thread is cheap and does measure curved lengths correctly. But it cannot be read at once: it has no markings, so it must be marked, straightened and measured on a rigid scale, whereas a flexible tape is read directly. So it is not better for every curved length.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: a thread can measure curved lengths
Wrong part: a thread must be straightened and read on a scale; a tape is read directly

questions.q:
A thread is laid once round the curved base of a bottle and marked. Mohit pulls it hard while straightening it, so the cotton thread stretches, and reads 23.4 cm on a metre scale. Meena straightens the same thread gently, without stretching it, and reads 22.5 cm.
(a) Which reading gives the distance round the base, and by how much is the other one off?
(b) A flexible measuring tape is then wrapped round the base. Which of the two readings should it agree with? Why?
questions.a: (a) Meena's 22.5 cm; Mohit's reading is 23.4 - 22.5 = 0.9 cm too long, because stretching made the thread longer than the curve it was laid on. (b) Meena's 22.5 cm, because the tape follows the curve and is read directly without being stretched, just as her unstretched thread kept the curve's length.
s: Part (a): 22.5 cm; the stretched reading is 0.9 cm too long
Part (b): the tape should agree with Meena's 22.5 cm, as neither is stretched

questions.q: A tailor has lost her cloth tape and must find the distance round a customer's waist today. She has a wooden metre scale, a long string, a rubber band and a 15-cm scale. Which method gives the correct distance?
questions.a: Wrap the string round, then lay it on the metre scale
o: Wrap the string round, then lay it on the metre scale
Hold the metre scale across the front of the waist, then double the reading
Put the rubber band round the waist, then stretch it along the metre scale
Lay the 15-cm scale round the waist piece by piece and add up the readings

questions.q:
Rohan wants the distance from his home to the market. He fixes a thin strip to a spoke of his bicycle's front wheel so that it clicks once each time the wheel turns. To find how far the wheel goes in one turn, he lays a string along the curved outer boundary of the wheel, marks it and straightens it along a measuring tape: it measures 1.8 m. On the way he counts 750 clicks.
(a) Why does he use a string, not a metre scale, to measure the wheel's boundary?
(b) How far is the market in metres?
(c) Express this in kilometres.
(d) If his string slipped off the tyre and cut across part of the curve while he was laying it, would his answer be too large or too small? Explain.
(e) If he misses some clicks while counting, would his answer be too large or too small? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The boundary of the wheel is curved and a rigid scale cannot follow it; the string can, and is then straightened and measured. (b) 1.8 m x 750 = 1350 m. (c) 1.35 km. (d) Too small: a string cutting across the curve is shorter than the boundary, so each turn would be counted as less than it really is. (e) Too small, because each missed click is a turn of the wheel that is not counted.
s: Part (a): curved boundary needs a string
Part (b): 1350 m
Part (c): 1.35 km
Part (d): too small, a string across the curve is short
Part (e): too small, uncounted turns

questions.q: Padma's bus passes a kilometre stone reading 'Jaipur 85 km'. It travels 38 km to a dhaba, then 9 km more along the same road towards Jaipur and stops. The kilometre stone at the stop reads 'Jaipur ___ km'.

On a straight road, the post office is 400 m from the temple, and Lata's house is 650 m from the temple in the same direction. A visitor standing at the post office asks the postman how far Lata's house is. The postman takes the post office as his reference point. What should he say?

Tara sits still on a wooden horse of a turning merry-go-round. Her mother watches from beside the fence.
(a) Name one reference point with respect to which Tara is at rest and one with respect to which she is in motion, with a reason for each.
(b) Her mother says, 'Tara is moving.' Tara says, 'I am not moving at all.' Who is right?
questions.a: (a) At rest with respect to the wooden horse (or the merry-go-round), since her position from it does not change; in motion with respect to the fence (or her mother), since her position from it keeps changing. (b) Both are right, each for her own reference point: Tara takes the horse, her mother takes the ground.
s: Part (a): one reference point for rest and one for motion, with reasons
Part (b): both right, for different reference points

questions.q:
For a sports-day relay, the teacher chooses a pole at the start as the reference point and wants stations at 15 m, 30 m and 45 m from it along a straight line. Station 1 has been measured from the pole and checked. A helper marks station 2 by mistake at 32 m from the pole, then measures station 3 as 15 m beyond station 2. The relay starts in 20 minutes.
(a) How far is the mistaken station 2 from where it should be?
(b) Where has the helper placed station 3, measured from the pole, and how far off is it?
(c) What did the helper do wrong in reference-point terms, and why did the error pass on to station 3?
(d) The teacher can re-mark all three stations from the pole (about 25 minutes) or move only stations 2 and 3 (about 5 minutes). Which should she do? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 32 - 30 = 2 m too far. (b) 32 + 15 = 47 m from the pole, 2 m beyond the correct 45 m. (c) He measured station 3 from station 2 instead of from the pole, the fixed reference point, so station 2's error was carried into station 3. (d) Move only stations 2 and 3, measuring each from the pole (30 m and 45 m). A full re-mark takes 25 minutes and would delay the 20-minute start by 5 minutes, while station 1 is already checked from the pole, so re-marking it adds nothing; the 5-minute fix is done in time.
s: Part (a): 2 m
Part (b): 47 m, 2 m too far
Part (c): measured from station 2, not the pole, so the error carried over
Part (d): move only 2 and 3 from the pole; a 25-minute re-mark would delay the start and station 1 is checked

questions.q: For a school fair, Meena marks the places of stalls along a straight path. Stall 1 is to be 10 m and Stall 2 is to be 20 m from her reference point, an ice-cream cart. At 9 am the cart stands 5 m from the gate and she marks Stall 1. By 10 am the cart has been pushed 3 m farther from the gate, and she then marks Stall 2. Meena says, 'Any object can be my reference point, so the cart is fine.' Check her claim, using the distances of the stalls from the gate.
questions.a: No. From the gate, Stall 1 is at 5 + 10 = 15 m and Stall 2 at 8 + 20 = 28 m, so they are 13 m apart instead of the planned 10 m: a 3 m error. Distances for marking places must be stated from a fixed object or point; the cart moved between the two markings, so its distances did not mean the same thing at 9 am and at 10 am. The gate, which does not move, would have been a proper reference point.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong for marking places
From the gate: 15 m and 28 m, 13 m apart instead of 10 m
A reference point for stating distance must be fixed; the cart moved, so the gate should be used

questions.q: Five friends argue about whether the library is nearer than the market. Two say the library, two say the market, and one says both are equally far. A map later shows that all five are right. What explains this?
questions.a: Each judged from her own house, a different reference point
o: Each judged from her own house, a different reference point
The library and the market move, so their distances keep changing all day
Each friend used a different body-based unit, such as her own stride
Distances cannot be stated at all without a metre scale or measuring tape

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If every row of chairs for an open-air function is marked by measuring from the front edge of the stage, a helper who arrives late can still place the remaining rows correctly.
Reason (R): Distances stated with respect to one fixed reference point mean the same to everyone who uses them.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
In a classroom, desks are in a straight line along a wall. Mona's desk is 6 m from the door, and the teacher's table is 2 m from the door, on the same line.
(a) How far is Mona's desk from the teacher's table?
(b) Mona tells a new student, 'My desk is 6 m away.' He walks 6 m along the line from the teacher's table and reaches the wrong desk. Explain what went wrong.
questions.a: (a) 6 - 2 = 4 m. (b) Mona did not state her reference point (the door), and the new student used the teacher's table as his; a position means something only when the reference point is named.
s: Part (a): 4 m
Part (b): the reference point was not stated, so he used a different one

questions.q:
A straight road runs from the bus stand past the school and on to a garden. Measured from the bus stand: school 1.0 km; Asha's house 2.0 km; Bala's house 2.6 km; Chetan's house 3.4 km; Dia's house 4.1 km; garden 5.0 km.
(a) For each friend, find the distance from her or his house to the school and to the garden.
(b) Which friends will say the school is nearer, and which the garden?
(c) Why do their answers differ even though no one has made a mistake?
(d) If all four measure from the bus stand instead, what do they say about the school and the garden?
(e) Justify why maps and signboards state distances from a fixed reference point.
questions.a: (a) Asha: school 1.0 km, garden 3.0 km; Bala: 1.6 km, 2.4 km; Chetan: 2.4 km, 1.6 km; Dia: 3.1 km, 0.9 km. (b) Asha and Bala: school nearer; Chetan and Dia: garden nearer. (c) Each measures from a different reference point, her or his own house. (d) The school is 1.0 km and the garden 5.0 km from the bus stand, so all four now agree that the school is nearer. (e) A fixed reference point gives everyone the same distances, so the information means the same to every reader.
s: Part (a): all eight distances
Part (b): correct grouping
Part (c): different reference points
Part (d): from the bus stand, school 1.0 km and garden 5.0 km, all agree
Part (e): a common reference point gives the same answer for everyone

questions.q: Students are marking a Kabaddi court, measuring every line from a pole they chose as their reference point. Halfway through, someone moves the pole 1 m to the left, and the remaining lines are measured from its new place. What will happen?
questions.a: Later lines will be 1 m out of place relative to earlier ones
o: Later lines will be 1 m out of place relative to earlier ones
Nothing, because every line is still measured from the very same pole
Only the first line will be wrong, because it was drawn before the move
All the lines will shift together, so the court will still fit the ground

questions.q: True or False? 'In a straight school corridor, the library is 12 m from the staircase and the science lab is 20 m from the staircase. So the lab must be 8 m from the library.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The two distances share the staircase as reference point but do not say on which side of it each room lies. If both are on the same side, the lab is 20 - 12 = 8 m from the library; if they are on opposite sides, it is 12 + 20 = 32 m away.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: 8 m only if both are on the same side of the staircase; 32 m if on opposite sides

questions.q: On a car journey along one straight road, Tara notes four kilometre stones in order: 'Delhi 92 km', 'Delhi 81 km', 'Delhi 70 km', 'Delhi 81 km'. Describe what the car did, using the idea of position with respect to a reference point.
questions.a: Delhi is the reference point. From 92 km to 81 km to 70 km the car's distance from Delhi was decreasing, so it was moving towards Delhi. Then the reading rose to 81 km, so the car turned back and moved away from Delhi, by 11 km.
s: Delhi identified as the reference point
Decreasing readings: moving towards Delhi
Rising reading: turned back, moving away by 11 km

questions.q:
Statement 1: A kilometre stone reading 'Delhi 60 km' gives a position using Delhi as the reference point.
Statement 2: An object is in motion whenever it is far away from the reference point.
Statement 3: A kilometre stone reading 'Delhi 60 km' tells a traveller that she has come 60 km from her starting point.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only

questions.q:
Padma's family travels by bus towards Lucknow. She notes three kilometre stones: 'Lucknow 128 km', then 'Lucknow 96 km', then 'Lucknow 64 km'. Her cousin, on a bus going the other way on the same road, sees the readings on the stones increase.
(a) Padma's brother thinks the stones show how far the bus has come from home. What do they actually show, and from which reference point?
(b) How far did Padma's bus travel between the first and the third stone?
(c) Which way is the cousin's bus going, compared with Lucknow?
(d) Padma's little brother says, 'Our bus is not moving at all, because the seats and I stay in the same place.' Is he right, wrong or partly right? Justify.
questions.a: (a) They show the bus's distance from Lucknow, which is the reference point, not the distance from home. (b) 128 - 64 = 64 km. (c) Away from Lucknow, because its distance from Lucknow keeps increasing. (d) Partly right: with respect to himself or the seats the bus is at rest, since their positions do not change; but with respect to Lucknow or the kilometre stones its position changes with time, so it is in motion. His answer is true only for the reference point he chose.
s: Part (a): distance from Lucknow, the reference point, not from home
Part (b): 64 km
Part (c): away from Lucknow
Part (d): partly right, judged for both reference points

questions.q: Kabir's bus is passing a kilometre stone that reads 'Agra 52 km'. His friend Rafi is on the same road, 15 km behind him, farther from Agra. What does the kilometre stone beside Rafi read?
questions.a: Agra 67 km

questions.q: Two lines for a race are already drawn across the school ground at 3 m and 13 m from the corner flag, along one straight line. The centre spot is 20 m from the flag on the same straight line, beyond both lines. Lina says, 'If we describe the lines from the centre spot instead, both numbers will change, and so will the gap between the lines.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. From the centre spot the lines are 20 - 3 = 17 m and 20 - 13 = 7 m away, so both numbers do change. But the gap is 13 - 3 = 10 m from the flag and 17 - 7 = 10 m from the centre spot: changing the reference point changes the numbers that describe positions, not the distance between the lines.
s: Verdict: partly right; the numbers change (17 m and 7 m)
The gap stays 10 m, so the distance between the lines does not depend on the reference point

questions.q: At a metro station, Rhea stands still on a moving escalator. A step of the escalator is taken as the reference point. Decide whether each is at rest or in motion, with a reason: (i) Rhea, (ii) her brother walking up the same escalator, (iii) a poster on the station wall.
questions.a: (i) At rest: her position from the step does not change. (ii) In motion: as he walks, his position from the step changes. (iii) In motion: the step keeps moving past the wall, so the poster's position from the step changes with time.
s: (i) at rest, with reason
(ii) in motion, with reason
(iii) in motion, with reason

questions.q: On a straight park path, a bench lies between a water tap and the gate. The bench is 30 m from the tap and 50 m from the gate. Which statement is NOT correct?
questions.a: The bench has two distances, so one must be wrong
o: The bench has two distances, so one must be wrong
The gate is 80 m from the tap, measured along the path
With the tap as the reference point, the bench is 30 m away
The bench is nearer to the tap than it is to the gate

questions.q:
Along a straight road, the school is 1.0 km from the bus stand and the park is 4.0 km from the bus stand, both in the same direction. Meera's house is 2.5 km from the bus stand, between them.
(a) How far is Meera's house from the school and from the park?
(b) A new shop is to open exactly halfway between the school and the park. How far will it be from the bus stand, and from Meera's house? What do you notice?
questions.a: (a) School: 2.5 - 1.0 = 1.5 km; park: 4.0 - 2.5 = 1.5 km, so both are equally far. (b) The school and park are 4.0 - 1.0 = 3.0 km apart, so halfway is 1.0 + 1.5 = 2.5 km from the bus stand. That is Meera's own position, so the shop will be next to her house, 0 km from it; (a) already showed her house is equally far from the school and the park.
s: Part (a): 1.5 km and 1.5 km
Part (b): 2.5 km from the bus stand, which is at Meera's house

questions.q:
In Sita's apartment block, heights measured from the ground are: 2nd-floor balcony 7 m, 4th-floor balcony 14 m, roof 20 m, top of the water tank on the roof 22.5 m. A plumber standing on the 4th-floor balcony takes it as his reference point.
(a) What are the positions of the roof and of the tank top with respect to him?
(b) What is the position of the 2nd-floor balcony with respect to him? What must he add to this number that the others did not need?
(c) A straight pipe runs up from the 2nd-floor balcony to the tank top. Find its length using the ground-based heights, and again using the plumber's numbers. What do you notice?
(d) The plumber writes on his job sheet only 'Leak at 3 m', meaning 3 m above his balcony. The next worker takes the ground as the reference point. How far from the leak will he look?
(e) Rewrite the job-sheet note so that anyone can use it, and justify your choice of reference point.
questions.a: (a) Roof: 20 - 14 = 6 m above him; tank top: 22.5 - 14 = 8.5 m above him. (b) 14 - 7 = 7 m below him; he must say 'below', because unlike the others it is on the other side of his reference point. (c) Ground-based: 22.5 - 7 = 15.5 m; plumber's numbers: 8.5 + 7 = 15.5 m. The length is the same; changing the reference point changes the numbers for positions, not the distance between two points. (d) The leak is 14 + 3 = 17 m above the ground, but he will look 3 m above the ground, which is 17 - 3 = 14 m below the real leak. (e) 'Leak 17 m above the ground' (or '3 m above the 4th-floor balcony'). The ground is preferred because every worker can start from it; a position means something only when its reference point is named.
s: Part (a): 6 m and 8.5 m above him
Part (b): 7 m below him, with below/above stated
Part (c): 15.5 m both ways; distance does not depend on the reference point
Part (d): leak is 17 m above the ground; he looks at 3 m, 14 m below the leak
Part (e): a note naming the reference point, preferably the ground, with reason

questions.q: A bucket is pulled straight up out of a well by a rope that runs over a pulley wheel. Which pair describes the motion of the rising bucket and of a mark on the rim of the turning pulley wheel?
questions.a: Linear for the bucket, circular for the mark
o: Linear for the bucket, circular for the mark
Circular for the bucket, linear for the mark
Linear for the bucket, oscillatory for the mark
Oscillatory for the bucket, circular for the mark

questions.q: Karan says, 'A swing changes its direction at each end of its path, yet its motion is still periodic.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. A motion is periodic if the object repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. A swing moving at a steady pace goes to and fro over the same path again and again, so changing direction at the ends does not stop it being periodic; the chapter states that oscillatory motion is periodic.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
Meaning of periodic: path repeated after a fixed interval of time
The swing repeats its to-and-fro path, so it is periodic despite turning back

questions.q: Of these four: a drawer pulled straight out once, the tip of a running ceiling fan blade, a raindrop falling straight down, and a cradle rocking to and fro at a steady pace, the number that show periodic motion is ___.

questions.a: (a) Oscillatory and periodic: the fan moves to and fro about a fixed position and repeats that path after a fixed interval. (b) Linear and not periodic: the ball moves along a straight line once and does not repeat its path.
s: Part (a): oscillatory and periodic, with reason
Part (b): linear and not periodic, with reason

questions.q:
A school fair already has a giant wheel and a swing boat that swings to and fro about its support. For Science Week the organisers want visitors to see all three types of motion. They can add one more ride: a toy train on a straight track (Rs 4,000) or a small merry-go-round (Rs 3,000). Their budget for it is Rs 3,500, but the principal will allow up to Rs 600 extra only for a ride that adds a type of motion not already at the fair.
(a) Which type of motion does each existing ride show?
(b) Which type of motion is missing at the fair?
(c) By how much would each new ride be under or over the budget?
(d) Which ride should they add? Justify, weighing the science aim against the cost.
questions.a: (a) Giant wheel: circular; swing boat: oscillatory. (b) Linear motion. (c) Toy train: Rs 500 over budget; merry-go-round: Rs 500 under budget. (d) The toy train. It adds the missing linear motion, so it qualifies for the principal's extra money, and Rs 500 over is within the Rs 600 allowed; the merry-go-round is cheaper but only repeats circular motion, so the aim of showing all three types would fail.
s: Part (a): circular and oscillatory
Part (b): linear
Part (c): Rs 500 over and Rs 500 under
Part (d): the toy train, since it adds linear motion and Rs 500 is within the Rs 600 extra

questions.q: In a children's park, which pair shows the same type of motion AND are both periodic?
questions.a: A see-saw rocked steadily, and a swing
o: A see-saw rocked steadily, and a swing
A child on a straight slide, and a raindrop falling straight down
A swing, and a giant wheel turning steadily round and round
A merry-go-round, and a ball rolled once down a straight ramp

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The free end of a metal strip held down on a table, pressed and released, shows oscillatory motion.
Reason (R): Both circular and oscillatory motion are periodic in nature.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A toy track is described in words. A marble rolls down a straight slope from P to Q, then goes once round a vertical circular loop that brings it back to Q, rolls along a straight level track from Q to R, and finally rolls into a U-shaped dip at R, where it rocks to and fro about the lowest point S several times before stopping. Name the type of motion on each part: P to Q, the loop, and the dip.
questions.a: P to Q: linear motion (straight line). The loop: circular motion (it moves along a circular path; going round only once, it is still circular). The dip: oscillatory motion (to and fro about the lowest point S).
s: P to Q: linear
Loop: circular
Dip: oscillatory

questions.q: True or False? 'The hour hand of a wall clock seems not to move at all, yet its tip is in circular and periodic motion.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Over an hour the tip's position with respect to the clock face clearly changes with time, so it is in motion however slowly it moves. It moves along a circular path and repeats that path after a fixed interval (12 hours), so its motion is circular and periodic.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: its position changes with time; it follows a circular path and repeats it after a fixed interval

questions.q:
Match each object in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. A seat of a giant wheel turning steadily  2. The pendulum of a wall clock  3. A stone dropped straight down from a bridge  4. The pole of a swing frame fixed in the ground
Column II: a. Moves to and fro about a fixed position  b. Moves along a straight line  c. Moves along a circular path  d. At rest with respect to the ground

At home Imran notices: the tip of a ceiling fan blade, a rocking chair rocking to and fro, a drawer being pulled straight out, and the pendulum of a wall clock.
(a) Classify each motion.
(b) Which of them are periodic?
(c) Compare the pendulum and the fan blade: how are their motions alike and how do they differ?
(d) Imran says, 'If I know a motion is periodic, I know it is circular.' Use (a) to (c) to judge his statement.
questions.a: (a) Fan blade tip: circular; rocking chair: oscillatory; drawer: linear; pendulum: oscillatory. (b) The fan blade tip, the rocking chair and the pendulum. (c) Alike: both are periodic, repeating their paths after fixed intervals. Different: the fan blade tip goes round a circular path, while the pendulum moves to and fro about a fixed position. (d) Wrong: the pendulum and the rocking chair are periodic but oscillatory, not circular; periodic motion can be either circular or oscillatory.
s: Part (a): all four classified
Part (b): three periodic motions
Part (c): alike (periodic) and different (path)
Part (d): periodic does not mean circular, with an example

questions.q: A tailor runs her sewing machine at a steady speed. Watching the needle, Ria sees it dip into the cloth and rise out of it, stitch after stitch, while the machine itself stays on the table. How is the needle's motion best described?
questions.a: Oscillatory and periodic

questions.q:
A boy rides a bicycle along a straight road.
(a) What type of motion does the bicycle as a whole show with respect to the road?
(b) A paint mark is on the rim of the front wheel. Taking the bicycle's frame as the reference point, what type of motion does the mark show, and is it periodic if the wheel turns steadily?
questions.a: (a) Linear: the bicycle moves along a straight line. (b) Circular: with respect to the frame the mark goes round the axle along a circular path again and again, so it is periodic.
s: Part (a): linear
Part (b): circular and periodic with respect to the frame

questions.q: Leela says, 'Every motion in a children's park is periodic.' Is she right? Use a swing, a merry-go-round and a straight slide in your answer.
questions.a: Partly right. The swing (oscillatory) and the merry-go-round (circular) repeat their paths after fixed intervals of time, so they are periodic. But a child sliding down a straight slide moves along a straight line once and does not repeat the path after a fixed interval, so not every motion in the park is periodic.
s: Verdict: partly right
Swing and merry-go-round are periodic
The straight slide is linear and not periodic

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A heavy box pushed along a straight floor shows linear motion.
Reason (R): In linear motion, an object repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
For a Science Week stall, Class 6 must keep one live example each of linear, circular and oscillatory motion running at the same time all day. They have one eraser tied to one thread, a thin 50 cm metal strip with a brick to hold one end on a table, and a toy car with a straight wooden ramp.
(a) What type of motion does the toy car show as it rolls down the straight ramp?
(b) Give two different ways of using the eraser and thread, and the type of motion each shows.
(c) What type of motion does the free end of the strip show when it is pressed and released?
(d) With only one eraser and thread, how should the stall use its materials so that all three types run at once? Justify using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Linear. (b) Whirled round: circular motion; hung, pulled slightly aside and released: oscillatory motion. (c) Oscillatory: the free end moves up and down (to and fro) about a fixed position. (d) Whirl the eraser for circular motion, use the strip for oscillatory motion and the car on the ramp for linear motion. The eraser is the only material that can show circular motion, while oscillatory motion can also come from the strip, so using the eraser for oscillation would leave no circular example.
s: Part (a): linear
Part (b): whirled is circular, hung and released is oscillatory
Part (c): oscillatory
Part (d): eraser for circular, strip for oscillatory, car for linear, because only the eraser can show circular

questions.q: A car's windscreen wiper sweeps to and fro across the glass about the point where it is fixed, again and again at a steady pace. How is the motion of the wiper best described?
questions.a: Oscillatory, because it moves to and fro about a fixed position
o: Oscillatory, because it moves to and fro about a fixed position
Circular, because the tip of the wiper moves along a curved path
Linear, because the wiper sweeps straight across the flat glass
Circular, because the wiper keeps coming back to where it began

questions.q: An orange falling from a tree and a clock pendulum both move downwards at some moment. Explain why the first is linear motion and the second is oscillatory.
questions.a: The orange moves along a straight line from the branch to the ground, so its motion is linear. The pendulum does not keep going in one direction; it moves to and fro about a fixed position, so its motion is oscillatory.
s: Orange: straight-line path, linear
Pendulum: to and fro about a fixed position, oscillatory

questions.q: True or False? 'A swing moves along a curved path, so its motion is circular motion.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. A swing moves to and fro about a fixed position; it does not go round a full circular path again and again, so its motion is oscillatory, not circular.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the swing moves to and fro about a fixed position, so it is oscillatory

questions.q:
Statement 1: A merry-go-round turning steadily shows both circular and periodic motion.
Statement 2: An eraser hung from a thread, pulled aside and released, moves to and fro about a fixed position.
Statement 3: A ball dropped from a height shows oscillatory motion because it moves downwards.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
In a children's park, Reena sees: a swing, a merry-go-round, a child sliding down a straight slide, a giant wheel, and a see-saw whose ends go up and down about the middle support.
(a) Classify each motion as linear, circular or oscillatory.
(b) Give the reason for the see-saw and the giant wheel.
(c) Which of the five are periodic?
(d) Reena puts the see-saw and the slide in the same group 'because both go up and down'. Explain what is wrong with her grouping.
questions.a: (a) Swing: oscillatory; merry-go-round: circular; slide: linear; giant wheel: circular; see-saw: oscillatory. (b) See-saw: its ends move to and fro about a fixed position (the middle support). Giant wheel: its seats move along a circular path. (c) The swing, merry-go-round, giant wheel and see-saw, since they repeat their paths after fixed intervals; the straight slide is not. (d) The types are decided by the path, not by the words 'up and down'. The child on the slide goes down a straight path once (linear, not periodic), while the ends of the see-saw move to and fro about the middle support again and again (oscillatory, periodic), so they belong to different groups.
s: Part (a): all five classified
Part (b): reasons for the see-saw and the giant wheel
Part (c): the four periodic motions
Part (d): slide linear and not periodic, see-saw oscillatory and periodic

questions.q: Which of these does NOT show periodic motion?
questions.a: A lift going once from the ground floor to the fifth
o: A lift going once from the ground floor to the fifth
The second hand of a wall clock that keeps good time
A see-saw rocked steadily by two children of equal weight
The needle of a sewing machine running at a steady speed
